facts.statement: Dallasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Turonian age.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Turonian),

facts.statement: Fossils of Dallasaurus were found in the Arcadia Park Shale in Dallas County, Texas, about 15 meters above the contact with the Kamp Ranch Limestone.
facts.quote: The genus is based upon two partial skeletons recovered from the Arcadia Park Shale (lower Middle Turonian), approximately 15 meters above its contact with the older Kamp Ranch Limestone in Dallas County in north-central Texas.

facts.statement: The type species Dallasaurus turneri was named after amateur collector Van Turner, who discovered the first specimen.
facts.quote: The first was found by an amateur collector, Van Turner, for whom the type species (Dallasaurus turneri) was named.

facts.statement: The genus name Dallasaurus honors Dallas County, the location where the fossils were discovered.
facts.quote: The genus is named for Dallas County, where both specimens were found.

facts.statement: The two known specimens of Dallasaurus were found approximately 100 meters apart.
facts.quote: The two specimens were discovered about 100 meters from one another

facts.statement: The fossil sites were temporarily exposed during housing development excavations and have since been reburied by construction.
facts.quote: The strata containing these fossils were temporarily exposed during excavations for a housing development, and both sites have now been reburied by construction.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen consists of an incomplete skull and postcranial skeleton representing about 80 percent of the animal.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen (TxVP 43209-1, Texas Vertebrate Paleontology Collections, University of Texas at Austin) consists of an incomplete and disarticulated skull, along with considerable portions of the postcranial skeleton, making up about 80 percent of the animal.

facts.statement: The second referred specimen lacks a skull and consists entirely of disarticulated postcranial remains.
facts.quote: The second referred specimen (DMNH 8121-8125, 8143-8149, and 8161-8180, Dallas Museum of Natural History) lacks any skull material and consists entirely of disarticulated postcranial remains.

facts.statement: The genus description is based on two partial skeletons found in the Arcadia Park shale in Dallas, Texas, near the contact with the Kamp Ranch limestone.
facts.quote: La descripción del género se basa en dos esqueletos parciales, recuperados de un manto de pizarra cretácica de la época turoniana, situado en Arcadia Park, Dallas (Texas), a unos 15 metros del contacto de esta placa con otra de piedra caliza denominada Kamp Ranch, famosa esta última porque de allí se extrajeron ejemplares de Russellosaurus.

facts.statement: Dallasaurus lived during the Upper Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico Superior

facts.statement: Dallasaurus is a basal mosasauroid from the Upper Cretaceous of North America.
facts.quote: Dallasaurus (Bell y Polcyn, 2005) es un género basal de mosasáurido del Cretácico Superior de América del Norte.

facts.statement: Dallasaurus is one of the smallest known mosasaurines, reaching approximately 1 meter in length.
facts.quote: It is also one of the smallest known mosasaurines, measuring approximately 1 m in length.

facts.statement: Unlike giant mosasaurs like Tylosaurus and Mosasaurus, Dallasaurus was similar in size to its living relative, the Komodo dragon, measuring less than a meter long.
facts.quote: A diferencia de otros mosasáuridos gigantescos, como Tylosaurus y Mosasaurus propiamente dicho, Dallasaurus era similar a su pariente vivo más cercano, el dragón de Komodo, de menos de un metro de longitud.

facts.statement: Dallasaurus likely lived an amphibious lifestyle, as plesiopedal mosasauroids were capable of terrestrial locomotion unlike entirely aquatic hydropedal mosasaurs.
facts.quote: While hydropedal mosasaurs were probably entirely aquatic, plesiopedal mosasauroids were still capable of terrestrial locomotion and so likely lived an amphibious lifestyle.

facts.statement: It is thought that Dallasaurus led an amphibious lifestyle because its limbs allowed it to move on land while it could also swim.
facts.quote: Muy probablemente, los mosasáuridos hidropedálicos eran totalmente acuáticos, mientras que los mosasáuridos plesiopedálicos todavía eran capaces de alternar entre el medio acuático y el terrestre porque sus extremidades les permitían la locomoción por el suelo firme. Así que puede pensarse que el Dallasaurus llevó un estilo de vida anfibio.

facts.statement: Cladistic analysis places Dallasaurus within the subfamily Mosasaurinae and the family Mosasauridae, excluding it from the paraphyletic family Aigialosauridae.
facts.quote: Bell and Polcyn have conducted a cladistic analysis of Dallasaurus, concluding that this taxon should be placed within the subfamily Mosasaurinae, "well within [the family] Mosasauridae", and that, despite its small size and the "primitive" condition of its limbs, it should not be placed within the paraphyletic family Aigialosauridae.

facts.statement: Dallasaurus belongs to the family Mosasauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Mosasauridae

facts.statement: Dallasaurus is classified within the subfamily Mosasaurinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Mosasaurinae

facts.statement: Dallasaurus was described by Polcyn and Bell in 2005.
facts.quote: authority: Polcyn et Bell, 2005

facts.statement: The genus name Dallasaurus refers to Dallas County, and the species name turneri honors the collector Van Turner.
facts.quote: El género lleva el nombre del Condado de Dallas, donde se encontraron ambos especímenes (Dallasaurus turneri: "lagarto de Dallas de Turner").

facts.statement: The popular press has described Dallasaurus as a "missing link" between fully aquatic mosasaurs and their terrestrial ancestors.
facts.quote: In the popular press, Dallasaurus has been hailed as a "missing link" uniting fully aquatic mosasaurs with their terrestrial ancestors.

facts.statement: A cladistic analysis by Bell and Polcyn in 2005 placed Dallasaurus within the subfamily Mosasaurinae and the family Mosasauridae.
facts.quote: Bell y Polcyn (2005, 188-190) han llevado a cabo un análisis cladístico de Dallasaurus, concluyendo que este taxón debe ser colocado dentro de la subfamilia Mosasaurinae, "bien dentro de la familia Mosasauridae"

facts.statement: Dallasaurus is related to other derived mosasauroids such as Clidastes, Prognathodon, Mosasaurus, and Plotosaurus.
facts.quote: Dallasaurus es entonces un taxón emparentado con otros mosasáuridos derivados, tales como Clidastes, Prognathodon, Mosasaurus y Plotosaurus.

facts.statement: Popular media has hailed Dallasaurus as a "missing link" connecting its terrestrial ancestors to fully aquatic mosasaurs.
facts.quote: En la prensa popular, Dallasaurus ha sido aclamado como un "eslabón perdido" uniendo sus antepasados terrestres a los mosasaurios plenamente acuáticos.

facts.statement: Despite its plesiomorphic limb condition, Dallasaurus should not be placed in the paraphyletic family Aigialosauridae.
facts.quote: a pesar de su condición plesiopedal no debe situarse en la parafilética familia Aigialosauridae

facts.statement: Dallasaurus lived during the Turonian stage, between 93.9 and 89.8 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Turonian to Turonian (93.9 to 89.8 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group of Dallasaurus is Mosasaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Mosasaurinae

facts.statement: Dallasaurus is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

rejected.quote: Junto con Russellosaurus, Dallasaurus es uno de los dos taxones de mosasaurios más antiguos hasta ahora conocidos de América del Norte.
